checkpoints: The loader's cache lives nowhere but inside the loader instance itself — so the instance's scope decides the cache's scope. That is why a request-scoped provider (Nest/Spring/ASP.NET) or a loader freshly built into the per-request context (Go) is a DELIBERATE choice, not an arbitrary implementation detail.

First failure of a process-wide singleton: stale reads — a later request reads back a key the loader loaded BEFORE an intervening write, because the old cached value is still sitting there, never cleared.

Second, and worse, an isolation breach: data loaded under one user's request context (their permissions, their tenant) can be handed straight to another user's request, because the loader itself has no idea who is asking — it only knows the key. Neither of these is a performance problem; both are correctness bugs.

The per-request cache actually exists to solve a very narrow problem: deduplicating load calls for the SAME key WITHIN one execution — batching already solves N+1 by width (many keys collapsed into one call), and this cache solves duplication by depth (the same key asked many times counts as one call). It is not, and was never designed to be, a general-purpose performance cache that outlives a single request.

Within one request, if a mutation writes to a key and the same key is re-read right after, the stale cached value (loaded before the write) would be returned unless something handles it — so right after the mutation, explicitly clear that key (or clear the loader's whole cache for that request) so the re-read is forced to hit the real data source again.

If the team genuinely wants the performance win of caching across requests, it has to be built on purpose — a dedicated caching layer (say Redis, or an in-memory cache with a TTL) with an explicit lifetime and invalidation whenever the underlying data changes — not by widening the loader's scope.
The loader's correctness depends exactly on dying with the request; making it a singleton trades correctness for a performance saving that isn't worth it.

Take five aliases of the same expensive field in one flat query: nesting stays at depth 1-2, comfortably under a depth-5 cap, but the server still has to resolve that field five separate times, so the real cost is five times one resolution, not one.
A depth limiter literally cannot see this, because "how deep does the tree go" and "how many times does the server do work" are different measurements — width lives on a different axis than depth.

Complexity fixes exactly that: give every field a declared cost reflecting how expensive it is to resolve, then sum the cost of EVERY field occurrence in the query, aliases included. Five aliases of a field costing 5 sum to 25; against a budget of 20 that query is correctly rejected, while the same query sails past any depth check.

Complexity checking needs only the parsed query's shape — which fields appear, how many times, and their declared costs — never any actual data or a resolver call; it is a pure walk over the query's AST.
That is exactly why complexity can be the PRIMARY gate: it is evaluated at the exact moment a query has been parsed and validated but before a single resolver has executed.

The payoff of gating there rather than after execution: a rejected query causes zero resolver calls, so the defence stays cheap for the server even while it is being actively hammered with hostile queries — and it should reject with a stable, distinguishable error code rather than a generic failure.

None of this works if cost assignment is sloppy: a field left undeclared silently defaults to a cost of 1, so an expensive list field that nobody bothered to price sneaks straight past the budget regardless of how large the list actually is — the fix is to price list fields and anything that touches a data source deliberately, ideally scaling that cost with the page-size or limit argument the client actually requested.

Complexity is not meant to stand alone: a rate limiter still caps how many requests a client sends per window (a different axis — volume, not per-query cost), a shallow depth cap still catches genuinely pathological deep nesting cheaply as a sanity ceiling, and for traffic from clients you fully control, pairing complexity with a persisted-query allowlist removes the guessing game entirely — only pre-approved query shapes execute at all.

DataLoader's batch function must return a result array of the exact same length and order as the keys array it receives, because DataLoader hands result[i] back to whichever caller invoked load(keys[i]) — matching happens purely by index, never by inspecting the content of the returned rows.

Grouping a flat SQL result set by iterating the rows themselves — rather than iterating the original keys array — produces an output ordered by whatever sequence the rows first appeared in, since an unordered SQL IN clause never guarantees it will return rows in the same order as the ids that were passed in.

An author with zero books contributes no group to a row-order-based grouping, so it doesn't just occupy the wrong slot itself — it silently deletes one array slot and shifts the position of every subsequent author's group by one index, compounding the misalignment for everything after it.

The batched query itself is correct and genuinely avoids N+1, which means this class of bug can hide behind SQL that looks completely fine — the defect lives entirely in how the batch function reshapes its query results back into the keys' order, not in the query.

The symptom is intermittent rather than constant because the misalignment only manifests when the database's row-return order diverges from the requested keys' order or a zero-books author sits among the batch; whenever the two orders happen to coincide, the mismatched code produces correct-looking output by coincidence.

A single-author query never exposes this bug because batching only ever contains one key, so there is nothing for that one result to be out of order relative to — it always lands at index 0 regardless of how the batch function grouped it, making single-key tests a red herring that masks the real defect.

The correct fix is to build an intermediate map keyed by each id while iterating the rows, then derive the final result by mapping over the original keys array and looking up each key in that map, falling back to an empty array for keys with no matching rows — this guarantees position i always corresponds to keys[i] and makes missing entries explicit instead of silently absent.

Verifying the fix requires asserting that every returned child record's foreign key matches its parent's id in a nested query, plus a regression fixture where an entity with zero related rows is sandwiched between two entities that do have rows, since that specific arrangement is what exposes an index shift.

`new PubSub()` from `graphql-subscriptions` creates an in-process object — `publish()` only reaches `asyncIterator`s that were instantiated inside the same running Node process, not across any process boundary.
On a single dev instance there is only one process, so the mutation's `publish` call and the subscription's `asyncIterator` are always the same object — every event is delivered with no exceptions.

Running the service as 3 replicas behind a load balancer means each replica boots its own copy of the service with its own private, unshared `PubSub` instance in memory — there are effectively three separate topics that happen to share the same string name.

A subscriber's WebSocket is a long-lived connection pinned to whichever replica accepted the upgrade, while each `createPost` mutation is a separate HTTP/WS request the load balancer is free to route to any replica independently.

An event reaches a given subscriber only when the replica that ran the mutation happens to be the same replica the subscriber's WebSocket is connected to; with 3 replicas and roughly uniform routing that coincidence happens about 1 in 3 times, exactly matching the reported symptom.

Sticky WebSocket sessions do not fix this bug: stickiness only pins the subscriber's connection to one replica, but does nothing to the mutation request, which remains a separate call the load balancer can still send to any replica.

The correct fix is to replace the in-memory `PubSub` with an adapter backed by an external shared bus — such as `graphql-redis-subscriptions`'s `RedisPubSub` — so that `publish` and every replica's `asyncIterator` all read from and write to the same external topic regardless of which replica handled the mutation.

The fix can be verified by running 2+ instances locally, opening a subscription against one instance while firing mutations against a different instance, and confirming every event still arrives exactly once with no duplicates once all replicas share the same external bus.

In a partial-update mutation, an absent field must leave the stored value untouched, a field sent as explicit null is a deliberate clear, and a field sent with a real value overwrites the old one — these are three distinct client intents the merge logic has to tell apart.

The nullish coalescing operator (`??`) cannot distinguish "field omitted" from "field sent as explicit null", since both are nullish — `input.publishedYear ?? existing.publishedYear` falls back to the existing value in either case.

Because of that collapse, a client can never actually clear a nullable field like `publishedYear` through this mutation, even though the field is declared nullable in the schema specifically so it can be cleared.

The correct fix is to branch on whether the key is present in the input (for example `'publishedYear' in input` or `input.publishedYear !== undefined`) rather than on whether its value is null: an absent key leaves the existing value untouched, while a present key — including an explicit null — overwrites with whatever the client sent.

`archiveBook` mutates the in-memory store yet is registered with `@Query` instead of `@Mutation`; query operation types are the part of the GraphQL contract that execution engines and clients are permitted to parallelize, prefetch, and cache.

Hiding a side effect inside a query field means it can fire more than once for a single client intent, or race against another field resolving in the same request, because the query contract carries no guarantee of single, serial execution.
Registering the operation as `@Mutation` instead restores the GraphQL guarantee that mutation fields run serially and are never cached or speculatively re-executed.

Locking in the corrected contract needs regression tests covering all three cases: an explicit null persists as null, an omitted field keeps the prior value, and calling a query-type field twice back-to-back leaves the store's state identical both times.

The server owns the money — full stop. Anything that travels through the client can be edited before it reaches the server, so if the charge amount comes from the client, there is no way to distinguish a real order from a tampered one.

The fix is that the client sends only a product id and a quantity; the server resolves each line against its own trusted catalog, computes the total in one single place, and rejects an unknown product id outright, because the client cannot invent a price for something the server has never heard of.

The client-sent expected amount is detection-only: it lets the server notice when the client's view of the world has drifted (stale cart or tampering) and reject that confirmation with a client error before any money moves or the gateway is ever called — the figure actually handed to the gateway is always the server's own computed ledger amount, never the client's proposal; the client can flag a discrepancy but never gets to decide the price.

Every amount is an integer in the smallest currency unit, because floating-point decimal arithmetic drifts (0.1 + 0.2 does not land exactly on 0.3) and that drift compounds silently across millions of transactions; the system adds and multiplies whole integers end to end, and only converts back down to a human-readable figure at the very last step, in the display layer, after every calculation has already finished.
Put together, this is one coherent trust model, not three unrelated rules: the server computes, the ledger records the lifecycle, and the client only ever proposes and reconciles.
A payment is not one API call, it is a lifecycle that moves from creating an intent, to confirming it, to landing on succeeded or failed, and the client is never in a position to shortcut that path.
States that the webhook endpoint is a public URL anyone can POST to, so without verification a forged payment.succeeded request could flip an unpaid order to paid

States that HMAC-SHA256 is computed over the signed message <timestamp>.<body>, and that only the party holding the shared secret can produce a valid signature (knowing the algorithm alone does not let an attacker forge one)
States the server verifies the signature FIRST, before parsing the payload, returning 401 immediately on a bad signature
States the comparison must be constant-time/timing-safe
Explains WHY: a plain equality check short-circuits on the first differing byte, so response timing leaks how many leading bytes matched, letting an attacker recover the signature byte-by-byte
States that a valid signature only proves the event was genuine once — it does not stop a captured valid webhook from being replayed later
States that because the timestamp is inside the signed message, the server can reject events outside a tolerance window (commonly ~5 minutes), shrinking the reuse window for a captured event
Concludes the trust boundary is the combination of all three — correct signing algorithm, timing-safe comparison, and fresh timestamp — not any single one alone

A guard that compares each incoming refund amount against the full captured amount in isolation, without subtracting already-succeeded refunds, lets multiple partial refunds each pass individually while their sum exceeds the captured total.

Three sequential refund requests, each for 60% of a captured amount, all pass an `amount > intent.amount` check because the check is evaluated against the static captured amount rather than what remains after prior successful refunds — the order ends up refunded 180% against 100% captured.

The correct guard recomputes remaining-refundable as the captured amount minus the sum of already-succeeded refunds pulled from the ledger, on every request, so a running total can never cross the captured amount no matter how many partial requests arrive.

Service-side idempotency only protects replays that reach the point where the key gets persisted to the index; a crash between the gateway call succeeding and that write leaves a retry with the same key invisible to the check, so the retry reaches the gateway again as a brand-new refund.

Forwarding the same idempotency key to the payment gateway call closes the crash-then-retry gap, because the gateway's own idempotency map then recognizes the repeated key and returns the original result instead of processing a second real refund.

Two-layer idempotency requires both layers to carry the key: the service layer dedups requests it has already recorded, and the gateway layer dedups calls it has already processed — guarding only one layer leaves the window between "gateway call succeeded" and "record persisted" unprotected.

Money operations sent over HTTP are not retry-safe by default; each idempotency or validation guard only covers the boundary it actually checks, so a fix touching just one layer still allows a duplicate charge or over-refund through the other layer's gap.

Two concrete tests confirm the fix holds: a sequence of partial refunds that sums past the captured amount must reject exactly the request that crosses the limit, and replaying the same idempotency key on an already-succeeded refund must return the identical refund record while the gateway shows exactly one refund was ever created for that key.

Running the confirmation email and fulfillment notification synchronously before the response is returned pushes total handler time past the payment gateway's delivery timeout; under at-least-once delivery semantics, the gateway reads a missed timeout as failure and redelivers the same webhook event.

Each redelivery re-enters the exact same slow synchronous path, adding more load onto an endpoint that is already struggling — the rising p99 latency and the pile of duplicate deliveries are not two separate symptoms but one self-amplifying feedback loop.

An idempotency check keyed on the event id stops the ledger transition from being re-applied on a duplicate delivery, but it does not stop a retry from re-paying the cost of the slow email and fulfillment calls or from occupying another request slot — deduplication alone cannot stop the retry storm.

The minimal work that must complete before the response leaves the handler is: verify the webhook signature, check idempotency by event id, and durably apply the ledger transition — nothing else belongs on that synchronous path.

Sending the confirmation email and notifying the fulfillment service are slow, non-critical-path operations that can be deferred to run after the 200 is returned (for example via a queue or background job), so their latency no longer counts against the gateway's timeout.

The 200 response may only be sent after the ledger transition has been durably persisted; acknowledging first and persisting second opens a window where a crash between the two loses the event permanently, since the gateway never redelivers a webhook it already received a 2xx for. Shortening the synchronous path does not remove the need for the idempotency guard — retries arriving during the transition window still have to be caught by that same check.

The contract that makes deferring the email and fulfillment work safe is that the gateway only needs confirmation the event was received and durably stored, not that it was fully processed end to end; that distinction is what separates a legitimate optimization from a correctness shortcut.

Confirming the fix worked requires checking that p99 ack latency stays under the gateway's timeout under load, replaying duplicate deliveries in a chaos test to confirm the ledger transition applies exactly once, and killing the process between the ack and the deferred job to confirm the durably recorded event lets the email and fulfillment work resume instead of being silently dropped.

A full-history join re-walked on every call makes cost scale with total ledger size rather than with how much activity happened between requests — a dashboard polling this endpoint every few seconds re-fetches and re-sums every intent's refunds from scratch even though only a handful of payments and refunds occurred since the previous poll.

Maintaining a per-intent totalRefunded as a stored running counter, updated in the same write path that flips a refund to Succeeded, replaces an O(intents x refunds) re-filter-and-reduce with a simple field read; keeping the counter rebuildable from the ledger via a periodic reconciliation job means a bug in the counter self-heals instead of becoming a silent, permanent lie in the report.

Caching the whole report as a versioned snapshot and invalidating it the instant a payment or refund write lands turns repeated full joins into a single reused computation, trading a few seconds of staleness for eliminating redundant work — an acceptable trade because the consumer is a dashboard poll, not a strict real-time feed.

Scoping the report by settlement period narrows the initial payment scan to one window instead of the entire ledger's history, since reconciliation is naturally periodic work and its cost should track the period being reconciled rather than the full lifetime of the ledger.

Across every optimization strategy, totalRefunded must keep counting only refunds with status Succeeded and every monetary sum must stay in integer cents with no floating-point rounding introduced — these correctness constraints cannot be relaxed just because the computation path changed.

ReconciliationService has to remain strictly read-only no matter how it's optimized; none of incremental aggregates, caching, or period scoping should turn it into a place that writes a corrected netAmount or any other figure back onto a payment record.

Because this report serves a periodic audit dashboard rather than a real-time feed, trading a bounded amount of staleness for much less repeated work — via caching or period scoping — is the right default, and full incremental real-time accuracy is only worth reaching for when a consumer genuinely can't tolerate any staleness.

Validating the optimization means running the new path against the original brute-force join over an identical ledger, including a mix of failed refunds to confirm they stay excluded, and checking that both per-line and aggregate netAmount match exactly before load-testing at the dashboard's real polling interval to confirm the latency improvement is real.
